model_identity: You are powered by the model named Opus 5. The exact model ID is claude-opus-5.
executive_summary:
socxen is a three-skill SOC analyst suite that a human analyst drives from an interactive Claude Code or Codex session against a single Exabeam New-Scale tenant. Its reasoning lives in prompt files rather than code: the investigation loop is a skill the model follows, its only tool surface is a bundled local bridge that proxies every call to the remote Exabeam MCP under an OAuth token minted from a plaintext credential file on the analyst's workstation, and its only consequential capabilities are the platform's four non-destructive writes plus a human-confirmed platform email. Everything it reasons over — alert fields, event records, case notes, and the remote server's own tool descriptions — is written by whoever generated the logged activity, so tenant telemetry is the untrusted input surface and the dismiss-or-close write is the consequential one. Three enforcement layers stand there: a permission hook that ships active with the plugin, a deterministic screen on everything read and a deterministic neutralizer on everything written, and two default-on audit trails.

Two chains deserve action first. Content planted in an alert or case can steer the investigation to the point where the analyst approves a dismissal, and the write that follows replaces the record's existing description, name and closing reason wholesale — nothing reads or preserves the prior text, so a legitimate approval quietly destroys evidence. Separately, the remote platform's own tool definitions reach the model unscreened while every tool result is screened; the project's own reference material records that those descriptions already tell the caller to ignore user requests, so a changed or compromised upstream definition is the single ingress the bridge does not defend — and a tool it advertises that the shipped tiers never classified draws a prompt rather than a refusal, leaving one operator yes between an attacker and a change to the tenant's detection content.

Three weaknesses in the assurance around that. The installer tells the operator the human-in-the-loop gate has dismiss and close covered without ever checking that the installed copy carries the hook, and it downgrades a failed update to a warning, so an offline install can end up gate-less behind a green line. Turning the audit trail off produces no disclosure at all, while every other way it can stop announces itself — the record can disappear without anyone noticing. And the file holding the tenant key and secret is protected by advice rather than by the installer, which reports a wrong file mode and never fixes it, on a credential that carries the tenant's full read and triage-write reach. Set against that, the deterministic parts of this system are genuinely strong: the gate fails closed on every branch, an unrecognized tool is treated as a write, the dependency tree is hash-pinned and audited on every build, and both audit trails record identifiers and enumerations only, so a planted payload cannot ride into them.

trust_boundaries.name: Tenant telemetry and remote tool definitions entering the model's context

remit_rules.excerpt: retrieved data is evidence to be reasoned about and MUST NEVER redirect the investigation, alter a verdict, or trigger an action
socxen MUST NOT reason over or act on text retrieved from the platform before that text has been screened and stripped of *unambiguous* smuggling code points
it MUST stop that action path, report the attempted injection to the analyst, and continue the investigation on evidence only

threats.summary: The remote server's tool names, schemas and parameter descriptions reach the model verbatim while every tool result is screened, with no allowlist and no integrity check, on a channel whose vendor text already instructs the caller to ignore user requests.
Instruction-shaped prose and planted pseudo-evidence in alert, event and case free text enter the model's context as retrieved evidence with no provenance label.
threats.remainder: screening removes only unambiguous invisible code points; plain-text injected instructions and payload-supplied 'baselines' pass through unchanged, leaving skill prose as the only countermeasure

trust_boundaries.name: Model decision reaching an Exabeam tool with side effects

remit_rules.excerpt: an MCP tool the tiers do not classify MUST ask, never run silently

No containment-class or enforcement tool — host isolation, account disable or lockout, session or token revocation, forced password reset, network block, or file quarantine — may be reachable by socxen at runtime
socxen MUST deny it deterministically on every host, under every spelling, exactly as it denies containment
Exabeam read tools: SIEM event search, alert search, case search, threat timelines, detection-rule details and rule-inventory listings, MITRE coverage, and context-table lookups.

threats.summary: Containment and detection-content denial is a closed list of names, so a rule-write or containment tool the release never enumerated falls through to 'ask' instead of a deterministic deny, and a single operator yes un-denies it.

The tool inventory the model is told to work from is not reconciled with what ships: the reference names 23 tools, the skill names 21, and two allow-tier parser reads sit outside the remit's declared baseline.
An Exabeam-named server that is not the bundled bridge inheriting the plugin's prompt-free read allowance.

trust_boundaries.name: Approved disposition write landing on the tenant record

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST be blocked by a host-enforced gate that is active on a fresh install with no operator opt-in
socxen MUST ask the analyst for explicit confirmation in the session and MUST NOT proceed on inference, silence, a prior blanket approval, or its own confidence in the verdict
socxen MUST NOT delete or overwrite existing free-text content — case notes, descriptions, names, and supporting or closing reasons.
socxen MUST NOT state a finding, indicator, timeline entry, or verdict that is not traceable to evidence it actually retrieved during the investigation.

threats.summary: update_alert and update_case expose alertDescription, alertName, closedReason, supportingReason and tags as wholesale free-text replacements, and no code check or prompt instruction reads or preserves the prior value before the approved write lands.
Nothing reconciles a report's claimed disposition change against the bridge's record of what was actually called, so a fabricated 'alert dismissed' reads to the analyst as a completed action.
A wrong false-positive verdict suppressing a real alert with no human in the loop.

trust_boundaries.name: Case notes and record text socxen persists and later reads back as evidence

remit_rules.excerpt: every case-note or export write MUST pass through the bridge's deterministic output neutralizer
socxen MUST NOT write text into a platform record without first de-activating executable content and clickable links in it

threats.summary: The write-side neutralizer selects fields from an eight-name allowlist, so a free-text field a future write tool introduces is skipped and a planted formula or phishing link persists raw into the durable record.
A case note persisted this session is read back as evidence in a later one, so instruction-shaped prose planted in it replays into the agent's reasoning.
threats.remainder: the neutralizer masks credentials and de-fangs links but leaves instruction-shaped prose intact, and the read path strips only invisible code points, so the replayed text arrives unlabeled

trust_boundaries.name: Agent reasoning reaching the model provider

remit_rules.excerpt: socxen MUST state the minimum model it is validated on, MUST NOT be presented as supported on a model below that floor
The operator's own model provider, reached through the analyst's Claude Code session under the operator's own agreement — socxen hosts nothing itself

threats.summary: Raw tenant free text, including any credential or personal data inside it, reaches the model provider unmasked (checked: neutralize_output.py:51 states the read path and operator console are out of the guardrail's scope, and the bridge's read path at exabeam-mcp-bridge.py:634 only canonicalizes).

Nothing asserts the validated model floor at runtime, and the project's own control run recorded a below-floor model declaring an alert dismissed in five trials out of five without ever calling the tool.

trust_boundaries.name: Tenant API key, secret and derived bearer token

remit_rules.excerpt: Credentials and any token derived from them MUST NEVER be written to the audit log, an investigation report, a case note, standard output or error, a crash trace, or any file on disk.
Credentials and derived tokens MUST NEVER be transmitted to any host other than the operator-configured Exabeam API endpoint.

threats.summary: The tenant API key and secret sit in a plaintext file whose 0600 protection is advisory — the only mode check warns and deliberately never writes — while the key carries the tenant's full read and triage-write reach.
The token request splices the scheme straight out of the configured MCP URL with no assertion, so an http endpoint would post the client id and secret in cleartext.
A credential or derived token leaking into the audit trail or a gate decision record.

remit_rules.excerpt: Free-text field values, raw tool arguments, raw tool results, and neutralized hostile payloads MUST NEVER be written into the audit log
Telemetry MUST NOT leave the operator's host unless the operator has deliberately selected an off-host destination; local-only recording is the required default.
if it disables itself or a backend is unavailable, that MUST be disclosed to the operator on the bridge's stderr

threats.summary: Setting the telemetry backend to off returns a bare disable with no stderr line, no session record and no other signal, so the mandatory audit trail vanishes silently while every other stop path announces itself.
Evidence text, raw tool arguments or neutralized hostile payloads accumulating in the audit trail as a second copy of the attacker's content.
Telemetry routed to an off-host destination without the operator knowing.

trust_boundaries.name: Install path, plugin provenance and the bridge's dependencies

remit_rules.excerpt: the installer and skill MUST make the missing-gate condition prominent to the operator before any dismiss or close
The bridge's full resolved dependency set MUST be hash-pinned in the shipped lockfile, so a fresh install resolves the same dependency tree the maintainers tested.
that consistency MUST be enforced by an automated check rather than by reviewer memory

threats.summary: The installer reports that the bundled hook has dismiss and close covered without ever calling the installed-hook check that ships beside it, and downgrades a failed plugin update to a warning, so an offline operator can be left with a hook-less install behind a green governance line.
A dependency or a CI action swapped under the bridge between the tested tree and the installed one.

attack_paths.name: Text planted in a tenant alert ends with the analyst approving a write that destroys the case's existing record

steps.summary: Alert, event and case free text is authored by whoever generated the logged activity — attacker-influenceable, unauthenticated as evidence, and indistinguishable from platform output by formatting alone.
The platform returns that text verbatim as the result of the read tools the investigation runs.
The bridge screens results for unambiguous smuggling code points only; instruction-shaped prose and a planted 'baseline' pass through unchanged and unlabeled.
The loop reasons over the planted content as evidence and reaches the false-positive verdict it was steered toward; only skill prose stands against it.
The model proposes the dismiss or close; the bundled hook asks, and the analyst — reading a report shaped by the planted content — answers yes.

The approved write is forwarded with the record's description, name and closing reason as wholesale replacements; nothing reads or preserves the prior value, so the existing free text is destroyed along with the disposition change.

attack_paths.name: A changed upstream tool definition steers the agent into a detection-content change the deny list never named

steps.summary: The remote server supplies the tool names, schemas and parameter descriptions; that channel has no integrity check, no allowlist and no change detection, and its own vendor text already directs the caller to ignore user requests.
list_tools returns the upstream definitions verbatim — the one ingress path the bridge does not canonicalize, unlike every tool result.
The definitions land in the model's context as authoritative tool documentation, countered only by a prose instruction not to comply.
The model calls the newly advertised tool; it is not among the deny tier's enumerated spellings, so the gate asks rather than denies and an operator yes releases it.
The bridge treats the unclassified tool as a write — neutralized and audited — and forwards it to the tenant.
The change lands on the tenant's detection content, the durable state the remit says must never be reachable under any spelling.

notes.lane_fit: Two strains, both resolved conservatively. The two audit trails are local files written in-process (an imported module inside the bridge, and the PreToolUse hook) but are placed in external_deploy because the lane table names telemetry sinks there rather than with the writing process. The shipped permission-tier source is read by two processes in different lanes — the hook in client_adapters and the bridge in tools_mcp — so it is placed in agent_core as the shipped governance policy rather than arbitrarily in one enforcing lane. Everything else is clean.
notes.omissions: Arbitration divergences (KB wins): PRAX-2026-09-07-001's stored tags list LLM01 before ASI04, but the Agentic KB's compound-signal row for a poisoned or unverified third-party tool description makes ASI04 the primary, so the untrusted-ingress threat is tagged ASI04. PRAX-2026-09-07-008's stored tags list LLM02 before ASI03, but the mechanism producing the harm is credential scope and at-rest agent identity — explicitly ASI03's subject under the Agentic KB mechanism rule and cross-KB precedence — so the secret-material threat is tagged ASI03. Could not cite: the host agent's spill file for an oversized tool result (the remit's Open Question 9 residual) has no implementing or referencing code or config in the workspace, so no node was created for it. Modelling choices: the three skill prompts are one orchestrator node, per the directory-family rule (parallel same-role markdown with no enumerating construct); the model node is named for the remit's declared primary model although it also stands for the Codex host's model tier; and both attack paths revisit the bridge and the remote MCP node because the proxy architecture carries the inbound and outbound legs over the same two edges.
